item.title: Recent DMT Hype Reawakens Old Philosophical Questions
item.description:
Psychedelics

Recent DMT Hype Reawakens Old Philosophical Questions

Is DMT unlocking the secrets of reality or just helping users escape this one?

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • DMT might reveal a new layer of human experience rather than a new reality.
  • It might not be possible to codify cryptic symbols that users report seeing while on DMT.
  • Anecdotes of DMT "trips" do not provide convincing evidence that we're living in a computer simulation.
3D structure of 5-AcO-DMT
Source: Wolren / wikimedia commons / CC-BY-SA-4.0

DMT (Dimethyltryptamine) is a powerful, naturally occurring psychedelic compound known for creating immersive visual and auditory hallucinations. It is found in various plant species and even in trace amounts in the human body. Many claim their experiences on DMT are not "hallucinations" but visits to another reality — one much more real than this one.

The conversations around DMT

YouTube podcaster Shawn Ryan's recent interview with independent researcher Danny Goler is one of the most fascinating conversations I've listened to in a long time. Goler, a 21st century DMT pioneer, pontificates on many philosophical topics including the nature of reality, human consciousness, religion and spirituality, and how taking DMT informs all of it.

Goler has disclosed that he's ingested DMT thousands of times and through his experience has come to a new understanding of this reality, which pales in comparison to the one DMT allows users a glimpse of. There are many "reveals" in the conversation that might sound absurb taken out of context. They include: 1) Thousands of people have reportedly seen "code" (like computer code or a cryptic and ancient language) in the walls using lasers while on DMT, and there's a project underway to create a Rosetta Stone of such symbols; and 2) what we take to be "reality" is rendered computationally and the physical world we're familiar with is an illusion.

DMT has been known about for a long time even in the clinical environment through pioneers like Terence McKenna and Rick Strassman, both of whom studied the compound's psychedelic effects in the later half of the 20th century.

What's interesting about DMT for someone interested in the nature of human consciousness is that it's produced naturally in the human brain (and other living systems) while other psychedelics like LSD, psilocybin, and ketamine are not. This fact might prove to be a clue to our understanding the DMT trip and whether it's actually showing us a new reality or just a new way of experiencing human reality.

DMT explorations invite some fundamental philosophical questions

Though the research into DMT is not new, its current renaissance seems tied to society's growing acceptance of psychedelic-assisted therapy. But some fundamental questions should be considered before we can entertain as true insight the sometimes outrageous claims made by its users. For example:

article continues after advertisement

1. A Different Reality? There is strong confidence among DMT users that the compound is granting them access to a different reality or at least another dimension of reality. But I wonder if this belief is founded. Is it possible to access another (veridical) reality simply by ingesting something into our human system? Aren't we still necessarily experiencing human reality with our particularly human apparatus even though it feels wildly different than what we're used to?

To employ a video game analogy: Is our ingesting DMT and temporarily experiencing reality differently akin to Pac-Man having the brief power to eat the predatory ghosts who are always chasing him only after ingesting a power pellet? Is it truly a different reality or just a brief excursion into a different way of experiencing reality?

2. Codifying Subjective Experience? Goler mentions a Rosetta Stone project that's underway to identify and codify the different symbols DMT trippers are seeing in the walls with the use of lasers. This project evokes the other minds problem from modern philosophy: How can we know that what you’re calling a "squiggle" instead of a "squoggle" manifests the same in my brain, i.e., that we’re actually seeing the same shape or having the same experience at all?

Philosopher John Locke famously pointed out that objects cause secondary qualities (like color, smell, and taste) that could vary from person to person, so even though we both call something "pink" it's possible you're experiencing green and I'm experiencing pink. There's no way to disprove this. So, since we cannot make this epistemological jump of shared experience even under normal conditions, how could we possibly make this inference with any confidence when the experiencers are under the influence of a compound known to cause hallucinations?

As an aside, it would be interesting to run some DMT studies with placebos. There's so much in the media now about people seeing code in the walls while on a DMT trip that I worry people might come to the experience with prepackaged tropes. Though such a study design with some participants receiving DMT and others receiving a placebo still runs into the other minds problem (i.e., there is no way to definitively prove what someone is experiencing with a placebo either!), this approach might begin to help researchers find consistency between seeing "something unusual" and seeing "nothing unusual."

article continues after advertisement

3. Evidence for the Simulation Hypothesis? Some DMT researchers, including Golen, have become convinced that the identification of code in the walls seen by DMT users during their trips is evidence that we're living in a computational world; or in other words, that what we take to be reality is actually a computer simulation. While I admit there are many avenues, both empirical and philosophical, that lead one to seriously consider the simulation hypothesis, I don't think seeing code in the walls while on a hallucinogen is one of them. Why not?

It seems far-fetched to believe that if we were living in a computer simulation, we would literally see computer code in the substrate around us since what's rendered by the code and the coding behind it are always at two different levels. The Pac-Man maze we see is not the programming lines of code behind it. I think it's more likely that DMT is hacking into something in the human brain that traffics in symbols and codes, maybe a mechanism or neuronal system related to language and communication, making users "see" code everywhere when that mechanism is triggered.

item.title: On the Subject of Surrender
item.description:
Spirituality

On the Subject of Surrender

Personal Perspective: Letting go creates space for growth, healing, and clarity.

Posted July 19, 2026

I chose this topic because the word kept coming up in my life, and I wondered if it is there in yours too, obvious or hidden. I looked the word up, of course. To surrender means to yield power, control, or possession of something, typically under pressure or demand. How has it come up for me? I can admit that I generally do not like to surrender, to give up control of my life. But that is coming up more and more for me, which is helping me to see when to keep fighting and when surrendering is smarter, more graceful, and sometimes the best way to get what you really want.

When Things Just Want to Stick

Let’s begin with frying pans. I always use nonstick frying pans but pay attention to the problems with their coating. This time I tried one that has a ceramic surface, given its superb reviews. I expect food in nonstick pans to start to stick when their finish starts to go, usually in a year or two. This one started to stick after three months. I wrote a complaint to the company but got no answer. So, for some weird reason, I gave that one away and bought another of the same kind. This time I was going to treat it really well.

Same story: After about three months, it started to stick when I was frying eggs or tofu, the very things for which I want a nonstick pan. I had to ask myself, could I still use it, but more carefully? I tried using a little more oil, keeping the heat lower, and keeping the contents moving, sliding around. This is working. I feel like I kind of surrendered to the pan’s needs, and it is giving back what I want.

When Parts of Me Want to Get Old

I am realizing that aging is also about trying to figure out when to fight and when to surrender. The doctors are certainly not into surrendering. I do seem to spend more time with them, discussing how to fight this or that. I do all I can to stay healthy and fit, but as I get older, I seem to have less energy, more problems. The increasing amount of time I spend on health stuff suggests that I am going to lose in the long run. Is that called death? I think so.

No, nothing is looking like death yet. But, for example, during the last few years at night, I have had pain on my right side, down near my spine. MRIs say my lower spine has degenerated. That's common and usually due to aging. To reduce the pain, I only sleep on my left side, but the pain often arrives anyway every few hours, and so I get up and do things that stop it for another few hours. My spine doctor has tried various shots and nerve ablations. Not much is helping in a permanent way. Long hikes and swims are how I stay fit, but they cause more pain at night. I am thinking more about “just living with it the rest of my life.” I think that is called surrender.

When Something Wants to Pound in My Head

A slightly trickier issue is that I have developed for the third time what is called pulsatile tinnitus. You hear your pulse, or the pounding of your blood vessels, in your ear. It only bothers me when I meditate, but that is a major “only” for me. The first time I got it was during my 2016 “pilgrimage to nowhere,” which I talked about in Spirituality through a Highly Sensitive Lens. For six months we travelled around North America and Europe, staying in each place for one month at a time, and one week of that was spent in extra hours of meditation. In the second month, walking in Sweden in a national park, I got both toes caught under a root and fell hard, face down, knocking my two front teeth in.

During the process of getting that fixed, a Swiss dentist put a gadget in my mouth for a long time, which later set off the pulsatile tinnitus. Given the importance of meditation to this trip, this loud constant pounding in my head really upset me. Transcending into silence seemed impossible. Every meditation was a struggle instead of being effortless. But good things happened. In France a few months later, I found an osteopath who cured it.

article continues after advertisement

Maybe five years later it came back. This time, there was a clinic in San Francisco that tried to treat it. First, they needed to know the cause, so they did MRIs. On the Friday night before Memorial Day Weekend, I was informed by the radiologist reading my MRIs that I have a “dissected carotid artery” and should go immediately to the emergency room.

Well, do not follow my example, but I did not go. I knew it would mean being up most of the night, and I knew there was nothing immediately wrong with me. Indeed, over the years they keep imaging that carotid artery and it just gets increasingly “dissected.” That MRI, however, ended the treatment plan, as they assumed the dissection was the cause of the pulsatile tinnitus and that could not be easily treated.

So, I had to surrender. I got better at dealing with the sound, using white noise to drown it out, and much later—I do not even know when—it stopped. Surrendering worked, I guess.

This third time, I have contacted that clinic again and am starting in on the MRIs. They say these days that it is important to find out the cause. So, we will look again, though I have little faith that they can treat it. But this third time I am totally surrendering to it, because of this next way that surrendering has entered my life.

When I Consider That I Am Not Really My Body/Mind

I am always interested in new ways of looking at awakening or enlightenment, even though my just-finished book on the topic is now published and cannot be updated. The latest view about it that I have given attention to (if you are curious, check out awakeningworld.net) is that “witnessing,” which is always involved in awakening, can arise in stages. First, you notice a silent, unbounded awareness more and more. I will write about this in a future blog. In the final stage, you identify with this infinite silent awareness as your real Self, so that this Self is the witness of your mind, body, emotions, and everything else in the world. So in a way, the small self or ego surrenders to the unbounded Self. As it is said, “I am That, thou art That, all this is That.” Pulsatile tinnitus is also That. This perspective really does make it possible to surrender to that pounding inside the head. (Although I will still let the doctors try to figure out the cause and treat it.)

article continues after advertisement

When Do You Surrender?

So, consider where you might need to surrender or even want to surrender. It is part of living, I think, but it especially can arise on a spiritual path. Just be careful not to surrender to anyone like a spiritual teacher or group. Surrender to the highest goal, and trust that you will arrive with the help of the highest helper.
